title: 1-to-1 Computer Initiatives: The Curious Case of Maine
author: Katherine Martinko
summary: Katherine Martinko examines the twenty-three-year natural experiment created by Maine's Maine Learning Technology Initiative, the first statewide 1-to-1 laptop program in the country, launched in 2002 and still running after more than $450 million in investment. Using pooled NAEP reading and math rankings across states, she shows Maine moved from being among the nation's top-performing systems before MLTI to roughly the middle of the pack in eighth grade and the bottom quartile in fourth grade by 2024, with its relative position worsening further after the pandemic despite two decades of device-saturated classrooms. She pairs this with a comparison case: neighboring Massachusetts, which never adopted a statewide 1:1 program and instead rose to and held the top national ranking for over twenty years. Martinko is careful to note correlation is not causation, but argues the pattern is consistent with what genuine EdTech research already shows -- 1-to-1 computing effect sizes (around +0.12) fall well short of the +0.42 threshold typically used to flag meaningful educational interventions -- and that after two decades the burden of proof belongs to those still promising transformation from devices alone.
points: 1-to-1 computer initiatives carry one of the lowest effect sizes in the EdTech research literature, roughly +0.12, less than a third of the +0.42 benchmark commonly used to identify meaningfully impactful interventions.

Maine, the first U.S. state to adopt a statewide 1:1 laptop program in 2002 and still running it after $450 million in investment, fell from a top-tier NAEP performer to the middle of the pack in eighth grade and the bottom quartile in fourth grade by 2024.

Massachusetts, which never adopted a comparable statewide device program and had far lower classroom laptop access than Maine, instead rose to and held the number-one national NAEP ranking for over twenty years during the same period.

Martinko explicitly declines to claim the data proves causation, but argues that after two decades and hundreds of millions of dollars, the burden of proof has shifted to those still promising that 1:1 computing transforms learning.
quotes: 1-to-1 computer initiatives have one of the lowest effect sizes in the entire EdTech literature: approximately +0.12. That's less than one-third of the +0.42 benchmark commonly used to identify educational interventions with meaningful impact.

Between 1992 and 2002, Maine ranked among the nation's highest-performing education systems, with both fourth- and eighth-grade students consistently placing near the top of the country. Following the launch of MLTI, however, Maine's standing began a long-term decline.
By 2024, Maine had fallen from one of America's highest-performing education systems to roughly the middle of the pack in Grade 8, and the bottom quartile in Grade 4.
In 2017, 55% of Maine eighth-graders reported having access to a laptop in all classes, compared with just 15% in Massachusetts.

Unlike Maine, Massachusetts' national standing did not gradually erode over the next two decades: it strengthened. By 2002, Massachusetts had risen to the top of the nation in fourth-grade achievement - and by 2003, it had done the same in eighth grade.

Maine began this experiment as one of America's highest-performing education systems - but today, its eighth-graders sit roughly in the middle of the national pack, while its fourth-graders have fallen to the bottom quartile. After two decades, surely the burden of proof belongs with those still making the promises.
